data.hypothesis: The correct fused candidate with up to 8192 partials measured 0.459449 ms, while the 16384-partial variant measured 0.473368 ms. This candidate keeps approximately 4096 elements per partial until the cap, then limits the count to 4096; at the largest input that halves finalizer fan-in versus 8192 partials but also halves first-stage CTA count. It tests whether the cheaper finalization offsets reduced large-input parallelism. No speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use this comparison to motivate a contrasting lower-cap experiment; it does not establish an optimal partial count.
memory_lessons.claim: The fused 8192-partial candidate was valid at 0.459449 ms, while the 16384-partial candidate was valid at 0.473368 ms. More partials did not improve the observed full-call time in that comparison.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure a 4096-partial cap with the same fused scalar-load and CUB reduction structure, validating all required cases.

data.notes: This preserves the fused two-stage structure with scalar input loads. Each launched first-stage CTA writes one current-call partial, and the finalizer overwrites output; the non-positive-size path also explicitly overwrites output with zero. Candidate correctness and full-call performance remain for controller evaluation.
transformations: Fuse fabsf(input[i]) into a first-stage block sum so no full-size absolute-value array or output initialization pass is needed.
Set partial_count to ceil(n/4096), capped at 4096; partition the input into contiguous CTA chunks and use scalar loads with a conventional 256-thread CUB BlockReduce.
Reduce all current-call partials in one final CTA and directly overwrite output; explicitly zero output for non-positive n.
